name: Song Dynasty
summary: A period of commercial and technological revolution: printing, gunpowder, the compass and the world’s first government-issued paper money.

knownFor.label: Magnetic compass
knownFor.note: Described by Shen Kuo for navigation.

location.value: China proper without the far north. Northern Song (960–1127) ruled from Bianjing (Kaifeng). Southern Song (1127–1279) held only the land south of the Huai River, ruling from Lin’an (Hangzhou).

terrain.value: The Yellow River plain in the north. The fertile, well-watered Yangtze and Huai basins and southeast coast in the south. The Grand Canal linked them.

climate.value: Monsoonal. The Southern Song relied on the warm, wet south for double-cropping rice.
climate.source: Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule: The Song Transformation of China (2009)

resources.value: Rice (including fast-ripening Champa rice), tea, silk, porcelain, coal and iron. Iron output was over 100 million kg a year, and coal replaced charcoal in blast furnaces.

disasters.value: Yellow River floods. In 1128 the Song deliberately broke its dikes to stop the Jurchen advance, causing a catastrophic change of course.
disasters.source: Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule: The Song Transformation of China (2009)

population.value: 80–110 million in the 1120s under the Northern Song, and about 65 million under the Southern Song (Wikipedia infobox, citing Chaffee 2015). The population roughly doubled between the 10th and 11th centuries.

urbanisation.value: Kaifeng and Hangzhou each had over a million people. Hangzhou grew from about 200,000 in the early 12th century to over a million a century later.

disease.value: No major Song-era epidemics are described in the sources checked.

migration.value: Mass migration south after the Jurchen conquest of the north (1127).

economicBase.value: A commercial revolution: market-oriented agriculture, iron and coal industry, porcelain, textiles, and booming internal and sea trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Maritime trade from Quanzhou and Guangzhou to Srivijaya, Chola India, Fatimid Egypt, Goryeo, Japan, Đại Việt and Champa, reaching the Indian Ocean and East Africa.

wealth.value: Wikipedia’s infobox gives GDP per person of about 26.5 taels. Some estimates call Song China the world’s richest economy at the time. Comparisons are very uncertain.

moneyAndTax.value: The world’s first government-issued paper money (jiaozi, Sichuan, 1020s; later huizi). About 6 billion copper coins minted in 1085. Wang Anshi’s New Policies reformed land tax and state monopolies.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Song dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

inequality.value: A wealthy merchant and gentry class grew. Land concentration and tax burdens pressed on peasants.
inequality.source: Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule: The Song Transformation of China (2009)

governmentType.value: An imperial monarchy run by a large civil bureaucracy recruited mainly through examinations (about 20,000 active officials). Civil officials were deliberately placed above generals.

keyRulers.value: Taizu (Zhao Kuangyin, 960–976, founder). Shenzong (1067–1085, backed Wang Anshi’s reforms). Huizong (1100–1126, artist-emperor captured by the Jurchen). Gaozong (1127–1162, founded the Southern Song). Zhao Bing (1278–1279, last).

succession.value: Hereditary within the Zhao family. Taizu was succeeded by his brother Taizong (976).

institutions.value: Civil service examinations as the main route to office (about 400,000 candidates by the late 13th century). Neo-Confucian (Zhu Xi) texts became exam standards in 1241. Song Ci’s pioneering forensic manual.

stability.value: Generally stable internally. Fang La’s peasant rebellion (1120) in Zhejiang. The main threats were external.

eliteConflict.value: Bitter factional struggles between reformers (Wang Anshi) and conservatives (Sima Guang). Opponents were exiled (e.g. the poet Su Shi). Cai Jing’s corrupt dominance under Huizong.

armyAndTech.value: A huge standing army, about one million soldiers at its height. A permanent navy from 1132. The earliest known gunpowder formulas are in the Wujing Zongyao (1044). Fire lances and bombs.

majorWars.value: Wars with the Liao (Chanyuan Treaty, 1005), the Western Xia and Đại Việt (1075–77). The Jin–Song wars and the Jingkang Incident (1127). Victory at Caishi (1161). The Mongol siege of Xiangyang (1268–73) and the Battle of Yamen (1279).

territoryChange.value: About 3.1 million km² in 980, falling to about 1.8 million km² by 1204 after losing the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 (Wikipedia infobox).

alliancesRivals.value: Paid the Liao and later the Jin to keep peace. Allied with the Jurchens against the Liao (1115–1125), which backfired. Allied with the Mongols against the Jin (1234), then was conquered by the Mongols.

inventions.value: Movable type (Bi Sheng, c. 1040). Gunpowder weapons. The magnetic compass for navigation. Paper money. Su Song’s astronomical clock tower. Pound locks on canals.
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Song dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

scienceEducation.value: Shen Kuo’s Dream Pool Essays. Growing private academies (e.g. Donglin, 1111). Mass printing spread books and learning.

openness.value: Very open to maritime trade and foreign merchants (Muslims in Quanzhou, Jews in Kaifeng), while politically on the defensive against northern states.

religion.value: Neo-Confucianism (Cheng Yi, Zhu Xi), Buddhism, Taoism and folk religion, plus Muslim, Jewish and Manichaean communities.

languageWriting.value: Middle Chinese. Classical Chinese in a flourishing print culture.

artsArchitecture.value: Landscape painting, Zhang Zeduan’s “Along the River During the Qingming Festival”, Song porcelains, ci poetry (Su Shi, Li Qingzhao), and Sima Guang’s Zizhi Tongjian history.

socialStructure.value: Emperor, scholar-officials and gentry (who ran local affairs), merchants, farmers, artisans. Women gained some property and inheritance rights.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong Han Chinese cultural identity formed in competition with the Liao, Xi Xia and Jin states.
sharedIdentity.source: Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule: The Song Transformation of China (2009)

neighbours.value: The Liao (Khitan), Western Xia (Tangut), Jin (Jurchen), Goryeo, Đại Việt and the Mongols.

ideasReligions.value: Printing, the compass and gunpowder spread west, and Song ceramics and trade reached the Indian Ocean. More Indian Buddhist monks visited than under the Tang (per Tansen Sen).

colonisation.value: Not an expansionist empire. It mostly defended its frontiers and paid tribute to northern states.
colonisation.source: Kuhn, The Age of Confucian Rule: The Song Transformation of China (2009)

riseSignals.value: Taizu reunified most of China over about 16 years. Civil government, examinations and a commercial and agricultural revolution followed.

peakPeriod.value: The 11th century for the Northern Song economy and culture. Southern Song Hangzhou was the world’s largest city in the 13th century.

declineSignals.value: Factional conflict and corruption (Cai Jing), the backfiring Jurchen alliance (1125), and loss of the north (1127). Later, the Mongols surrounded it after conquering the Jin (1234).

outcome.value: Conquered by the Mongol Yuan. Lin’an fell on 4 February 1276. The last emperor, the child Zhao Bing, died at the Battle of Yamen on 19 March 1279.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Song dynasty (checked 5 Nov 2026); video research: RESEARCH.md, “5,000 Years of China”

sources.value: The History of Song (Songshi), the Zizhi Tongjian, rich printed sources and local gazetteers, and archaeology (shipwrecks). Checked against Wikipedia on 5 Nov 2026. See also Kuhn (2009).

overallCertainty.value: Good, thanks to printing. Population and GDP figures are estimates. Some army and battle figures come from single sources.
